A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original copying and LTL experiments, including generalization, perturbation, limited-data evaluation, embedding sensitivity and hyperparameter analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds propositional-logic experiments, Llama evaluations, logic-task ablations and computational-efficiency measurements.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the shared/random embedding construction, resampling schedule, three random-vector generators, weight tying, normalization and sequence-adapted AdaCos with its scale cap of 100. Expanded explanations and additional task configurations do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: v3 adds propositional-logic assignment prediction using PropRandom35 and generated generalization and perturbation datasets (Section 5.3; Appendices C and G). Predicting possibly partial Boolean assignments introduces distinct task requirements beyond copying and temporal-trace generation, both of which are retained.

E2.justification: v2 compares three conventional-embedding baselines. v3 retains these and adds prompted Llama 3.2 3B comparisons on the logic benchmarks and generalization sets (Tables 2 and 8; Figure 6), substantially broadening comparator coverage. Figure 7 also adds a naive uniqueness-checking runtime comparator.

E3.justification: v3 introduces propositional-logic protocols, including order-insensitive assignment matching and a 132-dimensional, six-layer model trained for 50K steps. New LLM protocols use infix inputs, constrained JSON assignment outputs and top-k/top-p sampling; efficiency experiments add controlled timing procedures. Retained copying and LTL training settings in Table 4 match v2.

E4.justification: v3 adds normalization/AdaCos ablations on both logic tasks, propositional-logic perturbation tests and an LLM seed-sensitivity comparison. It also evaluates random-vector generation efficiency and revises the trace-generation scaling analysis. The copying ablations, embedding sensitivity and limited-data LTL study remain, largely relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: Appendix I newly specifies seed 42 for every LLM sample and reports comparison with an unfixed seed. Existing training-repeat counts, ten-draw embedding evaluations, standard deviations and correlation p-values are retained; no increase in those existing run counts is reported.

E6.justification: LTL generalization accuracies change from 92.37% to 90.76% for the proposed method, 47.07% to 41.97% for the vanilla baseline, 95.33% to 92.82% for full vocabulary, and 85.81% to 82.71% for alpha-renaming (v2 Figure 4; v3 Figure 3(a)). Their ranking and stated settings remain unchanged, without an explanation for the revisions. v3 adds substantial propositional-logic, LLM, ablation and efficiency results. It also replaces the trace-generation length-scaling curves with differently labeled evidence. Retained entries in Tables 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 match.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds a formal propositional-logic grammar, Equation 4, and defines the partial-assignment prediction problem. Existing alpha-equivalence, embedding and alpha-covariance definitions remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: Vocabulary generalization and alpha-covariance remain the central contributions. The rewritten abstract explicitly claims improved generalization over alpha-renaming across three tasks, and the introduction adds negligible computational overhead to its contribution statement. These extend the claims without redefining the central research contribution.

C2.justification: v2 briefly discusses in-distribution degradation and meaningful variable names. v3 substantially expands applicability limits to semantic information in natural language, manually specified interchangeable-token sets and training from scratch. It also adds interpretations of task-dependent normalization benefits, computational scaling and general-purpose LLM performance.

D1.justification: v3 adds its own code/project-page link, propositional-data generation details, and explicit normalization settings for the logic experiments. Appendices H and I disclose timing hardware and configurations, Llama quantization, Ollama version, sampling settings, output formatting and complete prompts. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v2.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for the Llama model family and py-aiger, and explicitly positions its language-modeling adaptation of AdaCos as previously unexplored. The related-work discussion otherwise remains largely intact; the Sanh and RoFormer publication updates concern existing cited works.

P1.justification: Detailed copying experiments move from Section 5.1 into Appendix E, where they are combined with the former hyperparameter-search appendix. The appendix structure is extensively reorganized, limitations are separated from the conclusion, the abstract is rewritten, and the introduction gains an explicit contribution list.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws Figure 2 annotations, moves the copying heatmaps to Figure 8, and combines LTL and propositional-logic heatmaps in Figure 3. It adds ablation, LLM and runtime figures, expands tables and adds prompt listings. The timing figure is rearranged vertically and replaces its two length-scaling curves with one.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical support by adding a second logic task and testing component necessity directly on both logic tasks, addressing v2's reliance on copying-task ablations. Efficiency measurements, reproducibility details and explicit applicability limits further improve the paper. The LLM comparisons remain contextual because training and inference settings differ, and the revised LTL averages are unexplained; these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.
